en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán of the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the phrase "listing the miscellaneous assembly," as for the expression "formerly called 'ordinary beings' (*pǎn*)," etc.:

for instance, the eight dragons were mostly bodhisattvas of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), and even those within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* have all attained inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*). Among these...
Regarding those who possess the Way, such as King Ajātaśatru and his retinue, how could they be merely ordinary worldly folk?
As for the "five realms," if there is no hell, it means that both the precepts and the vehicle have become lax.
Regarding the "two realms," there is no formless realm; this refers to those for whom the precepts are urgent but the vehicle is slow.
Regarding the "eight classes," they consist of the gods of the desire realm, the gods of the form realm, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, garuḍas, and humans, as detailed below.

Regarding the phrase "the Vaipulya [sūtras] enumerate the hells," this is fully explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) under the heading "Relaxed in Precepts, Urgent in the Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "transforming the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) into the formless realm," in the first fascicle of the *Zhongyin jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State), Chapter "The Division of Bodies," the Bodhisattva Niyatīrṣideva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How excellent is this teaching! It clarifies for sentient beings so that they may easily awaken upon hearing the Dharma."

Furthermore, there are those who are difficult to awaken, whether they exist in the realm of resistance (*sapratigha*) or the realm of non-resistance (*apratigha*), or are visible (*sanidarśana*) or invisible (*anidarśana*).

As previously mentioned, because there are both resistant and visible, as well as resistant and invisible [entities], the case of being visible and resistant is as explained before; the case of being invisible and resistant is like the *Keśarin* (Hairy) ghost, who reaches a place and smells its odor; the case of being invisible and non-resistant refers to other ghosts and spirits. Furthermore, they may exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). "With form" refers to the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form; "formless" refers to the lower three stages of the formless attainments (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, *vijñānānantyāyatana*, and *ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Although they are difficult to transform, the Buddha may go to them or bring them here.
The absence of this sutra [in certain versions] is merely due to omissions and the like; therefore, it is said that "one cannot apply a single rule" to all cases.
Furthermore, according to the detailed treatise on the relationship between the vehicle and the precepts, it is fully explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
Regarding the statement, "The ancients said that 'the person is the lord of the land,'" this refers to the assembly of King Ajātaśatru among the eight sections.
Since it is not employed here either, I have cited the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing) to refute it.
How could spirits and such beings necessarily require external guests?
As for the statement "not yet fully understood," although one might look to the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, the person need not necessarily come later; perhaps there is an underlying intention.
Regarding the phrase "ghosts and spirits reappear," this refers to the Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Asuras.

Regarding the phrase "the diversity of capacities," one should further say that various capacities differ; this includes the intermingling of analysis with essence, and the intermingling of the partial with the perfect, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “this is an explanation according to the teachings”: the Two Vehicles refer to the Two Vehicles of the two [lower] teachings; the Bodhisattvas refer to the Bodhisattvas of the three [higher] teachings. Since all three teachings possess the wisdom that issues forth into the provisional (*prajñā-niryūha*), and since it is said that the Buddha-way encompasses all as one—thereby being exclusively the Perfect Teaching—the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas both begin from the outset. Thus, the Buddha-way is precisely those who originally practiced the Perfect Teaching and did not come through the gradual stages.
Regarding the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) and the four kings of the three luminaries, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The Mount Sumeru has four terraces, each separated from the next by ten thousand [yojanas]. Extending outward, they measure sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively. The hosts of the kings Dṛḍhanemi, Mālādharin, Sadāmatta, and Mahārāja dwell on the four levels in order. They also reside on the other seven mountains. At the summit of Sumeru, eighty thousand [yojanas high], dwell the Thirty-three gods. At its four corners are four peaks where the Vajra-headed ones reside. In the center is the palace named Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in circumference. It is adorned outside by four gardens: Caitraratha, Pāruṣyaka, Miśraka, and Nandana."

If one establishes the four *siddhāntas*, the dwelling place is termed the "world" (*loka*); that which can bestow benefit is for "persons" (*pudgala*); reflecting on the meaning is "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*); and the Lord of Devas is the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the provisional teachings: the *Āgamas* testify to the Tripitaka, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* testifies to the Shared [Teaching].
Regarding the Distinct and Complete [Teachings]: since Śakra appears in the second stage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, we know it is clear that both of these two teachings attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Regarding the phrase "beyond the Bhadrakalpa" and so forth, it is fully explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā* [sūtras].
As for the term "and so on," the meaning of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "together partaking of ambrosia" found in the *Benji* (Prolegomena and Traces), the sixth chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," states:

"Just as the Heaven of the Thirty-three possesses the wondrous ambrosia, the medicine of immortality," which serves as a metaphor for the identical principle shared by those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
Regarding "Named Moon" and so forth, both the original and the manifested [teachings] appear in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the original [teaching] must necessarily involve instruction.

As for the "meaning of contemplative understanding," the three truths are themselves the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*). The truth is the object; the object gives rise to wisdom, and wisdom is like the child.
The phrase "and so forth" means that because objects differ, cognitions differ, and thus the resulting mental states are not the same.
"Dwelling on the four jewel mountains" refers precisely to Mount Sumeru;
as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Each of the four terraces has ten abodes," as detailed in the *Xuanwen*.

Regarding the statement "twenty-four thousand *li* wide," its source is unknown; however, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it rests upon the middle slope of Mount Sumeru and has four terraces. As the verse states:
"Extending outward sixteen thousand, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively," because each successive terrace above is reduced by half.

Regarding the passage beginning with "East Dhṛtarāṣṭra" and so forth, its title appears in the second chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings. At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa presided over the directions starting from the east and ending with the north.
In the third chapter, "On Ghosts and Spirits," twenty-eight divisions are listed.
Regarding the phrase "not allowing" and so forth: the traces [of the Buddha] guard the four trees; since these four trees symbolize the four virtues, the traces manifest the fundamental.

Although the fundamental guardianship of the four virtues at the twin trees involves both the four withered and the four flourishing aspects, the principle that is neither withered nor flourishing does not transcend the [four] of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, guarding the eight trees is to guard the four virtues.
There are two meanings to "protecting the four virtues":
first, one must not take them partially, for taking them partially constitutes deviation;
second, one must not take them entirely, for taking them entirely constitutes attachment.
One must understand that its principle is neither withering nor flourishing.

What is now called "branches and leaves" refers to the fact that within a single virtue all four virtues are fully present; if one were to grasp only one name, one would not know that it encompasses all virtues. Thus, they are termed "branches, leaves," and so forth. Consequently, these names appear in non-Buddhist teachings as well. Therefore, when the text states, "The trunk and branches are metaphors for the eternal," and so on, it is precisely to reveal that each single virtue possesses all four virtues.

Regarding "protecting against the eight types of craving and views": beneath each of the Truths (satya), there is one instance of craving and one of view. Within the fourfold sets of the Four Truths, each according to its respective teaching, these cravings and views are eliminated; thus, the Four Kings each take charge so as not to allow people to be overwhelmed, just as they each protect against views and cravings so that they do not seize upon external objects.
If explained from the latter perspective, "King" refers to the King Samādhi (*rājasamādhi*).
Both the teaching and the teacher may be considered "kings," as each destroys craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the phrase "the five desires of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin [heaven]... and so forth, one should fully explain the physical dimensions and lifespans of the gods of the desire realm.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits; for those of the eastern, western, and northern continents, it doubles successively. For the gods of the desire realm, one *krośa* increases by one-quarter at each level. For the gods of the form realm, the first four levels increase by half a *yojana* each; above these, they double successively, except that the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*) reduces this by three [yojanas]. Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the lowest heaven (Cāturmahārājakāyika); based on this, their lifespan is five hundred years. For the five higher heavens, the lifespan doubles successively. In the form realm, there is no distinction between day and night; their lifespan in kalpas is equal to their body size. In the formless realm, the first two levels have twenty thousand great kalpas, increasing by twenty thousand for each subsequent level. For the gods from the Lesser Light (*Parīttābha*) upward, a full or half kalpa constitutes a kalpa."
Regarding the discussion of heights and depths for each respective heaven, the distance to the upper limit is equal to the distance from the lower limit.

In the sixth fascicle of the *Alternative Translation of the Āgama*, it is explained in detail how various Brahmās descend; in the eighth and eleventh fascicles, it is extensively explained how various devas praise the Buddha. When devas come, they all assume human form. The fourth fascicle states:

"When the Brahmā King came to pay homage to the Buddha, the Buddha had entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), so [the Brahmā] could not approach him and instead went to the gate of Kokālika to call for him."
Kokālika asked:
"Who called you?
He replied:
The Brahma King asked again:
"Has the Buddha prophesied that you will attain the stage of Anāgāmin?"
Answer: It is so.
Again, he asked:
"One who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not return'; why have you come?
The Brahma King replied, "One such as this should not be spoken to."
Thus we know that, although the rules for human beings are uniform, there are still instances where they conflict with worldly sentiments, as seen in the admonition to Kāli.

Regarding the phrase "there are likewise gates of teaching" and so forth: since he is the master who requested the Wheel of Dharma for the entire dispensation, when he requests the Great [Vehicle], it is the Great; when he requests the Small, it is the Small.

Regarding the "Original and the Traced" (*honjaku*): the Original resides in the pure, single reality of the wondrous realm. Through contemplation, the removal of delusions and defilements is also termed "purity.

Furthermore, within the text, among the various devas who come forth, only Śakra possesses the four [qualities] of the Śakras; as for the devas of form such as the Three Lights, the Four Kings, and Maheśvara, although they have their own causes and conditions, they are all excluded from the provisional teaching (*kyōkyō*). Nevertheless, since these devas constantly follow the World-Honored One everywhere to hear the Dharma, one should likewise judge their depth or shallowness and their revelation according to the flavor of each respective teaching. This is like the case of Śāriputra receiving his prediction of enlightenment; however, because the matter of propagating the teachings is slight, I have merely cited this as an example.
Therefore, while the eight dragons mostly follow this pattern, only the *Jin* [section] provides explicit instruction, as it is more convenient for the meaning.

Regarding the "immeasurable dharma-gates" followed by "and so forth," because there are many aspects, we take the contemplation of the provisional (*jia*) as the primary focus; that is, one provisional [aspect] entails all things being provisional.
If explained generally, "one is empty and all are empty" and "one is the center and all are the center" also have multiple aspects.
Regarding the *Dīrgha Āgama* and other texts, those sūtras fully clarify how a lake gives rise to the four great rivers, as described in the *Commentary*.
"A" means "non-existent," and "nir" means "affliction"; it is because he is free from those three afflictions.

Regarding "the original abiding *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*": everything realized through the true path is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, but for now, I am merely using the flower to explain the flower.
Regarding the "four *kiṃnaras*," the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"They are included within the realm of animals; the *kiṃnara* has one horn, while the *kiṃpuruṣa* has no horns, though their bodily forms are roughly similar."

Regarding the current statement, "Presenting the four teachings," and so forth: since all five flavors have their respective partial and complete [teachings], one should know that what is presented likewise distinguishes between the partial and the complete; thus, it has come down to this present sutra alone to reveal the ultimate truth.

As described in the *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the Kinnara King Mahādruma, together with immeasurable kinnaras, immeasurable gandharvas, and immeasurable devas, played eighty-four thousand pure and wondrous musical notes as they approached the Buddha’s dwelling. As the strings and songs were set in motion, their sound shook the great trichiliocosm; Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, surged, submerged, rose, and fell, while all the śrāvakas rose from their seats as if performing a dance.
The Bodhisattva Diademed asked Kāśyapa,
"One who is foremost among those who have few desires, are content, and practice the dhūta austerities, yet today acts like a small child.
Kāśyapa replied:
This was not their original intention.

Therefore, we know that the aforementioned sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (fangděng) section, which uses the Great Vehicle to censure the Small; it is like the Kinnaras playing the music of the Distinct and Complete Teachings, causing the Śrāvakas to be unable to remain at ease. Thus, when one reaches the Lotus Sutra, it is logically fitting that the principle be purely sublime.
Regarding the "Ten Jewel Mountains," they are fully enumerated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as already recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, it first lists seven mountains, together with Mount Sumeru, making eight.
The *Śāstra* states:

"Sumeru stands in the center, followed by Yugandhara and the others; outside the great continents lies the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountain. The first seven mountains are composed of gold, while Sumeru consists of four jewels; together with the Himavat and Gandhamādana mountains, these constitute the ten mountain ranges."
Since it is said that he performs music for the sake of the devas, and since the capacities of these devas also differ,
the phrase "singing the praises of the Ten Powers" implies— given that he does not arise from the meditative concentration of cessation— that he has already attained the first stage (prathama-bhūmi).

Therefore, within the traces [of the past], the stringed instruments and pipes should also sing of the four teachings, each possessing the ten powers. For instance, in the *Mahāvṛkṣa-sūtra*, after the Buddha accepted an offering at the south of Mount Gandhamādana, he prophesied that the donor would attain Buddhahood under the name Guṇarāja; by principle, this must have been a prophecy concerning the Dharma-body.

If one were to receive the prediction of the eight signs at the first stage (prathamabhūmi), it would still pertain to the provisional traces; the content of the present sutra does not exceed that of the *Mahāvṛkṣa-sūtra*, because it is not easy to hear this Sutra of Reality.

Furthermore, the reason why the Dragon King now cites eight [qualities] and the Kinnaras and others four each is because there is a symbolic significance; the number eight corresponds to the Eightfold Noble Path, as each of the various teachings possesses its own version of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Since the four teachings have already been summarized, their general purport can be understood.

As for the remaining items, worldly music uses the mundane to represent the ultimate truth; the four *gandharva* instruments are explained according to their respective meanings in relation to the teachings.
"Banner" (*dhvaja*) refers to the banner of conditions, which is the *pāṇava* drum.
"Upside-down" refers to being cast down and so forth.

Regarding the four types of rebirth, they are also called "without gods" because they lack divine virtues; the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* classifies them under the divine category, while the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* classifies them under the categories of ghosts and animals. When a Great Power manifests such a transformation, to which specific conditions and determinations does it correspond?
According to the *Āgamas* and other sources, the four abodes of the *asura* clans are situated at the bottom of the ocean, each measuring twenty thousand *yojanas*.
As for the phrase "the various kinds of *asura* devas," this refers to their primordial progenitors.
Regarding "the five fetters that bind the Māra-heretics," this is fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

As for the "five abodes" (*pañca-vāsana*), other interpretations hold that they are merely the views and afflictions within the realm of desire; if that were so, how would they differ from the four abodes?

He said: "The views of the three realms constitute the Dwelling Ground of Views (*dṛṣṭi-ekadeśa-vāsa-bhūmi*); the volitions of the desire realm constitute desire-love (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*); the volitions of the form realm constitute form-love (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*); the volitions of the formless realm constitute formless-love (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*); and the ignorance of the three realms constitutes the Dwelling Ground of Ignorance (*avidyā-vāsa-bhūmi*). However, according to the Five-Nature School (*pañca-gotra*), the seeds of views, doubt, ignorance, and so forth are taken as the Dwelling Ground of Ignorance."

Now, my view is not thus: the five abidings serve as the cause for the two types of death; specifically, the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms constitute the four abidings, with the addition of the specific afflictions (*āveṇika-kleśa*) as the fifth abiding. Therefore, within the specific afflictions, both internal and external ignorance, as well as the ignorance within the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), are collectively contained.
The *Wei shi* (Vijñaptimātratā) and other such works differ from this only by the addition of the "seeds" (*bīja*).
As for the term "Original Text," it refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "crystal entering the body":

this may refer to either a sentient being or a non-sentient entity; if it refers to a non-sentient entity, its meaning is equivalent to moisture-born birth (*saṃsvedaja*) while also encompassing the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), as in the *Āgama-sūtras*, where it is recorded that a woman warmed herself by a fire, and through the entry of warmth into her body, she became pregnant.
The father, suspecting her, rebuked her, and the matter eventually reached the king, who intended to punish her.
The girl said, "How can there be such an unrighteous king who wishes to punish an innocent person? I pray that Your Majesty will test me."
The King, knowing she was innocent, took her as his consort.
This is detailed exactly as recorded in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
Regarding the phrase "the fundamental purity of form and mind," it is stated in contrast to the superficial manifestations of ugliness and jealousy.
Because the primordial abiding form (*prakṛtistha-rūpa*) is pure, prajñā is pure; because prajñā is pure, the mind is pure.

Regarding the phrase "this is called the sustaining of obstructions," it means that [prajñā] is able to sustain and maintain the obstructions; the worldly claim that there is a "constant sustainer" lacks any basis.
Regarding "solar eclipses": if one were to entirely deny that worldly phenomena exist, why is it that they can nonetheless be predicted through calendrical calculations?

This is because the laws of the physical world (bhājana-loka) naturally accord with the principles of human yin and yang; thus, the five elements within the human body correspond to the numerical cycles of heaven and earth. Consequently, the laws of waning and waxing must correspond to the calendar; how could this interfere with one's primary spiritual practice?

Regarding the phrase "various heterodox teachings": although the sun and moon illuminate the four continents, and the four continents likewise possess differing patterns of yin and yang, could it be that by failing to allow them to wane and wax, one causes all kings and others to utterly decline?
The same applies to calamities such as floods and droughts;
therefore, one should know that while one portion [of these phenomena] accords with the principles of yin and yang, another portion must depend upon the karmic power of sentient beings.

Therefore, all environments that rely upon a land necessarily accord with the primary retribution; for instance, the Flower Treasury Land (Huazang) must accord with the Buddha of Retribution and the various Bodhisattvas. This sovereign mastery over both the primary and secondary [retributions] applies equally to skillful means.
Regarding the phrase "fearing the sun, moon, and time," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states:
"When Rāhu desired to devour the moon, the Moon Devaputra fled in terror and appealed to the Buddha, speaking in verse:

'O Greatly Wise and Diligent Buddha, World-Honored One, I now take refuge in you and prostrate myself before you. This Rāhula is tormenting me; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant me protection.'"
The Buddha spoke this verse for Rāhu:

"The moon can illuminate the darkness and bring coolness; it is the great lamp of brightness in the void of space. Its color is pure white with a thousand rays; do not swallow the moon, release it quickly!"
At that time, Bhañjī saw Rāhu sweating as he released the moon, and asked him in verse:
"O Rāhula, for what reason do you tremble so violently, as if afflicted by illness and fear, remaining so ill at ease?"
Rāhu replied:
"If I do not release the moon, my head shall split into seven pieces; even if I were to survive, I would find no peace. For this reason, I now release this moon."
Regarding the phrase "formerly a brahmin" and so forth, as the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The desire-realm devas [start at] one-fourth of a krośa, increasing by one-quarter for each level up to the sixth heaven, which is one and a half krośas. Since it is said that their body height is eighty-four thousand yojanas, this would still place them at the very top of the form realm; given that the lifespan in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is sixteen thousand kalpas and the body height is sixteen thousand yojanas, they must be able to manifest a transformed body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of eighty-four thousand yojanas.
Regarding the phrase "fond of battle" and so forth: when these four asuras engage in war with Śakra, they deploy their armies in succession, arranged exactly as they are listed here.

According to the eighteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there is a Vajra Mountain in Jambudvīpa, within which lies the palace of the asuras; its domain extends for six thousand yojanas, complete with railings and rows of trees. Yet, three times every day and night, they suffer torment, and instruments of pain spontaneously enter their palace. This is truly why they belong to the four evil destinies.
The third volume of the *Alternative Translation of the Āgamas* extensively explains the battle between the asuras and Śakra; those who require it should consult it there.
If one were to establish the meaning based on the teaching (*śāsana*), it may also be done according to the names [of the deities]; I shall now do so.
First, regarding "the five bonds": this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching, who are fully endowed with the five stages (*bhūmi*).
Next, "broad shoulders" refers to those of the Shared Teaching, as their general contemplation of the three vehicles is somewhat more extensive.
Next, "pure mind" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching, who first realize true purity.
Next, regarding the phrase "obstructing and maintaining": this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), who obstruct delusions while maintaining the Principle.

As for the passage beginning with "The Original Contemplation," it is omitted here as there is no time to discuss it in detail; however, it may also be explained as follows: In essence, they abide in the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-dhātu); in their manifested traces, they demonstrate the absence of such heavens. Because they can contemplate that which is immediately empty, there are no humans or devas of the Three Realms. Because they are immediately provisional (prajñapti), there are no heavens of the meaning of the Land of Expedient Means (Upāya-bhūmi). Because they are immediately the Middle Way, there are no heavens of the meaning of the Land of True Reward (Dharmatā-vipāka-bhūmi). Through the three contemplations in a single mind, they eternally dwell in the Quiescent Light (Sada-prabhāsvara), a state of being neither human nor heavenly—a "human-deva" beyond both human and celestial categories.
Regarding the passage in the *Four Āgamas* which states, "In one's own dwelling there is a palace," and so forth, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18, says:

"To the north of the great ocean is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves extending fifty yojanas. To the east of the tree is the palace of the egg-born nāgas, and also the palace of the egg-born garuḍas. To the south is that of the womb-born, to the west the moisture-born, and to the north the transformation-born; each has its respective palaces for nāgas and birds. All possess seven rows of trees where various birds sing in harmony. When seizing a nāga, the wings strike the ocean waters: the egg-born strike open [the sea] for two hundred yojanas, the womb-born for four hundred, the moisture-born for eight hundred, and the transformation-born for one thousand six hundred. Following this sequence of womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born, they consume one, two, three, and four nāgas respectively."

"Thus, when these abodes of the evil realms are compared to the Western World of Peace and Bliss, one knows that blessings are easy to attain while precepts are difficult, and precepts are easy while the vehicle is difficult; this is because those who do not return [to the world of suffering] are so few."

Furthermore, as the *Āgama* states: "On Mount Gandhamādana there is an elephant named Supratiṣṭhita, who always dwells beneath trees. He has six tusks, upon which there are ponds and other features; his appearance is nearly identical to that of Samantabhadra’s elephant. There are eight thousand such trees and elephants, with Supratiṣṭhita as their king and the others as his retinue. Some hold parasols, fans, or water-jars; some perform songs, dances, and music; others wash the king, and so forth."
"What of this evil path? "Āo (pronounced with the *qie* of wǔ and dāo) and sàn (pronounced with the *qie* of sī and dāo). "Tán" means to devour;
"tán" is pronounced with the *qie* of tú and làn.
“Vajra Mountain” refers to the southern part of this continent.
“The mountain of jewels about to burn” means that the fire is about to reach other mountains of gold.
If explained according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), the initial statement that it “surpasses the multitudes” is because it transcends all non-Buddhists (*bāohài*).
Next, it is called "Great Body" because it is the beginning of the Mahāyāna;
next, it is called "Great Fulfillment" because one has fully emerged into the provisional realm;
and it is called "As One Wishes" because it is fulfilled according to principle.
Next, the assembly of people is listed: "Vaidehī" is also called "Victorious Thought.

Regarding "Ajātaśatru," while his mother was pregnant with him, she already harbored an evil mind toward King Bimbisāra; because he was already wicked even before birth, he was given this name accordingly.

Regarding "No Finger" (Aṅgulimāla): when he was first born, the physiognomists declared him to be an ill omen. The king ordered him to be thrown from a high tower; however, he did not die, but merely lost one finger, which is how he received his name.
Regarding the "Eight Dharmas," they may refer to the eight wrong paths (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*), the eight winds (*aṣṭa-vāyu*), or the eight inversions (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*).
As for the *Puchao jing* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence), its third chapter, the "Chapter on Resolving Doubts" (*Jueyi pin*), states:

"The Buddha, for the sake of King Ajātaśatru, who had broken his resolve and was certain that he committed the sin of patricide, extensively explained that throughout the three periods of time the three minds are unobtainable, thereby causing him to abide in the Dharma-realm."
"Upon hearing this, King Ajātaśatru attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of accordance with truth).

Regarding the phrase "when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," it is because his attainment of *anulomikī-kṣānti* occurred prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; while he was among the pure assembly during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the sores on his body only began to manifest at the time of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. He then repented for having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and thus we know that [his attainment of patience] was merely intended to lead those who had committed the crime of parricide.
This is entirely an interpretation based on great expedient power (*mahopāya*), which is why Kāśyapa is cited as an example.

If one were to interpret this according to actual practice, although it is said that [Kāśyapa] was pure during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he had not yet obtained benefit; by logical inference, one should say his hindrances had not been removed and his spiritual capacity (*indriya*) had not been activated. It was only upon reaching the time of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that his hindrances were about to be removed and his capacity had already been activated;

thus, hearing the Buddha’s prediction, he attained realization and rejoiced, subsequently speaking verses in praise of the Buddha. Therefore, the seventeenth chapter states: "The Father King was falsely and unjustly subjected to treacherous harm... until my heart was filled with remorseful fever and sores broke out over my entire body. There was no skilled physician in the world to heal my body and mind. Disbelieving the words of the six ministers and the six teachers, I followed the instructions of my elder brother Jīvaka. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I received the prediction and made a vow."
"You should know that both of these places are merely traces; what opposition or compliance could there be within their fundamental ground?
Furthermore, it is like the brahmin named Ahimsaka (Non-Harming), who was called Aṅgulimāla because he had killed immeasurable sentient beings."
It is because they have seen the Buddha that they resolve their minds on Bodhi.

Furthermore, in Vārāṇasī there was the son of an elder named Ajita, who killed his father, harmed his mother, murdered an Arhat, and set fire to a monastery; later, wishing to leave the household life, he was not ordained by the bhikṣus, yet he himself resolved his mind on Bodhi—this is another such example.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind, it destroys the "mother of craving" and so forth, as cited from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in the commentary to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the statement "practicing what is not the Way" and so on, the contrary is itself the compliant, and that which is not the Way is itself the Way.

Furthermore, "path" (mārga) has the meaning of "thorough penetration. Because the principle realized can thoroughly penetrate contemplative wisdom, leading from cause to fruit, it is called the "path. Even the minds of the nine realms are termed "non-paths," let alone a mind that is contrary [to the Dharma].
Someone asked:

"If, according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, even those who merely bow their heads or raise their hands can all attain the Buddha-way, how is it that King Ajātaśatru’s grave offenses were not extinguished?

It is simply necessary to rely on the four propositions regarding the movement of the faculties and the removal of obstructions, to judge the sequence of maturation over time, and to understand that the conditions for transformation follow the individual's capacity; there is no need for such a question."
The subsequent question may be understood from the context.

Although the response cites the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, according to reason one should further cite the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra*; for among those who attain the Way, numbering as many as the dust motes of the four continents up to the great trichiliocosm, how could there not be various classes of human beings within them?
Therefore, one should know that this is merely a brief summary.

Regarding the statement "a single phrase is expanded into four phrases" up to "as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*," that work explains the four phrases through seven meanings: first, clarifying the differences between the vehicles, the precepts, and the meeting with a Buddha; second, the differences between the two practices of faith and dharma; third, the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; fourth, the gradual and sudden capacities of the faculties; fifth, the manifested traces [of the Buddha]; sixth, the contemplation of the mind; and seventh, the transformation of others.
Regarding the initial mention of "vehicle and precepts": if one possesses the vehicle, one encounters the Buddha; if one lacks the vehicle, one does not come [to encounter him].

As for those who believe in the Dharma, whether they practice seated meditation or listen to and study the lectures, they all encounter the Buddha; it simply depends on whether what they have practiced is of the Great or Small Vehicle.
Regarding "gradual and sudden," this is because both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess gradual and sudden approaches.

Regarding "manifesting traces," having attained the twenty-five samādhis to correspond to the twenty-five states of existence, he leads practitioners of the ultimate truth to the presence of the Buddha.
Regarding those who contemplate the mind, they determine whether they see the Buddha solely based on their contemplative practice.
Regarding those who transform others, whether they see him or not is determined entirely by the benefit conferred upon others.
The manifestations of great expedient means are roughly as described in the present text.

Regarding the phrase "If one attains," etc.: these four lines are able to distinguish whether oneself or others encountered the Buddha at a particular time or place, and whether the attainment of the Way was swift or protracted. By examining the presence or absence of various examples across the sutras—such as the number of assemblies—one may verify the place of one’s own future rebirth, just as a seal leaves no discrepancy. When one reflects on this and reproaches oneself regarding the preface of the sutra, how could one not feel shame before the True Teaching?
Next, the separate introduction (pṛthak-nidāna) is explained according to the text of the third fascicle.

As for the term "separate introduction," it receives its name in contrast to the general introduction (sāmānya-nidāna); furthermore, this is stated from the perspective of mutual comparison within the specific teaching itself.
The Buddha and his disciples can be understood through the two passages, one preceding and one following the sutra.
Furthermore, if one follows the Tathāgata’s final testament, then the general introduction (sūtra-piṭaka) applies universally, while the specific introduction applies only to the particular [sutra].

If the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world and his arrival until the present are distinguished from the past within this sutra, then the meaning of this specific introduction (nidāna) is distinct yet simultaneously comprehensive; it is comprehensive because it recounts the past, and thus pertains exclusively to the present sutra.
The text of the general introduction is comprehensive while its meaning is distinct; it is distinct because it pertains to the present, and thus applies universally to all sutras.

If we directly address the distinction between the general and the specific regarding the introductory sections: the text of the general introduction is general and its meaning is general, because the section encompasses all teachings; yet there is also a case where the meaning is general while the intent is specific, as the specific distinctions lie within the various "flavors" (rasa) of the teachings.

The text of the specific introduction is specific and its meaning is specific, because it does not pertain to other sections, such as the incident of holding the bowl with the lid joined, which pertains specifically to the present sutra;
yet there is also a case where the meaning is specific while the intent is general, because it applies generally to all teachings.

Furthermore, the general introduction (sāmānyanidāna) may be common [to multiple sections] while its meaning differs, because it varies according to the number of teachings addressed in each respective section;

the specific introduction (viśeṣanidāna), on the other hand, is distinct [to each section] while its meaning is common, because it universally describes the number of teachings within that particular section. This is done in order to fully encompass both the common and the specific.

In the introductory sections of other sutras, the names of the two parts correspond to their respective contents; however, in the present sutra, while the first part generally recounts the past, the second part provides a double account of the preaching of the Dharma and the gradual and sudden illumination of the radiance. Only the "Flower-Earth" section exclusively expresses the intent of this scripture, as its meaning was previously undisclosed. The entry into meditative concentration involves both opening and closing in its significance; the "Joy of the Multitude" reflects a movement of delight distinct from the past, contrasting the former with the present. The "Doubtful Thoughts" section takes both the past and present as objects, while wavering regarding the future. The "Questions and Answers" section extensively recounts the three identities, comprehensively encompassing the entire dispensation. Since the intent of the sutra is profound and the introduction is likewise extraordinary, other sutras proceed directly to the formal commencement [without such detailed preliminaries].
"At that time" refers to the moment when the six auspicious omens were about to manifest.
When ancient scholars say it refers to the time when the assembly had gathered, they fail to grasp the intended meaning of the words.

Generally, the phrase "at that time" indicates the conclusion of a preceding event and the beginning of a subsequent one; here, it points to the period before the manifestation of the six omens, at which time the assembly was first surrounding the Buddha as he was about to preach the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.

If one says "when the assembly has gathered," one cannot say "the assembly surrounds [the Buddha] at the time of gathering. This is as in the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, which refers to the moment when Mañjuśrī has finished answering the questions; it cannot be said that this is "when the Buddha arises from samādhi.
As for "arising from samādhi," expressions such as "after that" or "only then" all refer to the period subsequent to that time.

If the assembly has already gathered, one may say that he then preached the *Anantārthadharmaparyāya*; thus we know that in a specific sense, this refers to the time when he was about to preach the *Anantārthadharmaparyāya*, whereas in a general sense, it may point to the period before the Buddha had definitively decided to arise [from his meditation].
At the beginning, the fourfold assembly surrounded [the Buddha], and even flowers rained down and the earth shook; thus it says, "At that time, the heavens rained," and so forth.
The reason for repeating "At that time, the heavens rained" is to specifically indicate the period following his entry into meditative concentration.
Although this is a minor matter, its precedents are indeed numerous; as the matter is not insignificant, it is intended that one should recognize it thoroughly.
"Turning over" refers to the preceding [discussion of] the inverse and the direct.

To proceed from the beginning toward the end is called "forward" (anuloma); to reverse this and proceed from the end toward the beginning is called "backward" (pratiloma). Regarding the term "arising" (*utpāda*):

proceeding from the beginning toward the end means that what precedes is born and what follows arises; proceeding from the end toward the beginning means that what follows is born and what precedes arises. Thus, answering by means of "birth" is based on the question concerning "arising," and it may also be said that answering by means of "arising" is based on the question concerning "birth. This applies equally even to the assembly of the factors (*samudaya*).
Although he permits both the "contrary" and the "conformable," his intent is to refute the lack of a central principle; thus he says, "not yet manifest.
What is this principle?
It refers to the manifestation of the "four and one," for nothing revealed by this sutra transcends these four. This, moreover, uses the principles of Guangzhai to refute Guangzhai.
According to our own school’s perspective, eleven [aspects] should be manifested.

Regarding the phrase “It is simply,” etc., this criticizes his method of interpreting the text; for while he manages to grasp one meaning of the world within the causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) through either direct or inverse order, he lacks all three of the remaining [meanings]. Therefore, it is said that he “does not even understand them himself.”
"Furthermore, two, three, and four" refers to the three [categories] beginning with the teaching.

Regarding the section "Now, clarifying... and below, which directly addresses the fourfold "one" within the context of the Fourfold Benefit (catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu), it signifies that these four "ones" should be understood as identical. Thus, one knows that throughout the beginning and end of this school’s tradition, the essential meaning has been grasped: the "one person" is the world, because many people harmonize together and continue to remain the same;
the "one principle" is the ultimate truth (paramārtha), for this name most perfectly accords with the six auspicious omens, each of which does not fail to manifest the central significance.

The first type of practice is for the sake of persons; through the cultivation of practice, one brings about the welfare of sentient beings, resolving doubts and giving rise to thoughts so that all deeds may be accomplished.

The second type of teaching is for the purpose of remediation; because doubt is removed through answering questions, the teaching arises—thus, question and answer constitute the teaching for the removal of doubt.

This has been a brief discussion of its general principles; however, when the assembly gathers, each individual possesses the fourfold "one," and it is only through this manifestation that [the practice] can arise, for there is a basis for both the inverse and the direct sequences.

If it were not so, why would no Mahāyāna sūtra fail to assemble the assembly, emit rays of light, rain down flowers, and shake the earth? Why, instead, does [the Buddha] merely give rise to great doubt in them, rather than requesting [Mañjuśrī] to answer? And why, in answering the question, does he not cite the three "samenesses"?

Although it has not yet been explicitly taught, it is known through the process of questioning and answering arising from doubt; thus, prior to the Flower Land (Puṣpabhūmi), the teaching was already established as being extraordinary, and before that definitive teaching, the assembly did not gather in vain. Although they had previously heard the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, because they did not disperse once the teaching was settled, they knew that what they had heard earlier was not yet complete. Therefore, we know that after the Flower Land, the definitive teaching that arose was not insignificant. By comparing the preceding and succeeding stages, the Flower Land itself must also be distinct. Consequently, the hearing of the Dharma manifests the person of the One Vehicle, and the manifestation of auspicious signs by those persons reveals the principle of the One Vehicle. To clarify this principle, questions and answers arise; thus, the teaching and practice reside in the person, while the principle remains perfectly manifest.

Furthermore, the auspicious omens signify that the opening of the sutra represents the convergence of the teachings, entry into the samādhi of convergence represents the manifestation of practice, the emission of central light represents the manifestation of the central principle, the raining of flowers represents the manifestation of the central stages, and the shaking of the central earth represents the removal of central delusions; thus, they collectively constitute the single person, for which there is indeed a profound reason.

Therefore, "Heaven" refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha), and "Earth" refers to the ground of the true nature (dharmatā). Although both possess manifest signs, the assembly of that time could not fathom them; thus, even upon hearing the opening of the sutra, they did not yet know that the opening fundamentally signifies union, let alone being able to understand the fixed principles and so forth.

Therefore, it was only by waiting for Mañjuśrī to lead them forth that they came to know the transformative teachings were no different; thus we know that the arising of doubt was fundamentally intended to establish practice. Once doubt is resolved, practice is perfected, and one realizes that the ancient teachings cited are identical to the present ones. Only then does one know that the Buddha is now proclaiming the oneness of the teaching, thereby enabling those in the assembly to become followers of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). In this way, the present sutra serves as a gradual path, acting as the initial sprout for the manifestation of ultimate reality.

If it were not so, then to merely speak of "explaining the introduction" would fail to manifest the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* itself; such an approach remains nothing more than an "explanation by way of causes and conditions.

Within the context of the "Exposition of Teachings," one ought to clarify the bestowal (*śe*), opening (*kai*), abolition (*fei*), and convergence (*hui*); only then will that which is manifested in the introduction become evident. As for the statement that "[it is] not a treasury (*piṭaka*) and so forth," this is said to be "not" in both cases because the provisional is abolished; for the principle is such that abolition must precede opening.
Therefore, although the three [vehicles] are simplified through the successive teachings, they are not yet called "One"; once the revelation is made, there is nothing that is not the King of Sutras.
Furthermore, since what is revealed is exclusively the Perfect [Teaching], it is said to be "not" [the others].
Thus, one pre-emptively distinguishes the capacity for revelation without discussing the *piṭakas* and so forth; the same principle applies to the meanings of the five flavors and the four flavors.
Interpreting it in this manner still pertains to the Gate of Traces (*jimen*).

To indicate the Gate of the Origin (*honmon*) by means of "distinguishing between origin and trace," one must wait until the *Nyorai Juryō-hon* (Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Life Span), yet it may also be indicated in advance here; thus we know that this introduction explicitly indicates the four aspects of the Trace and implicitly indicates the four aspects of the Origin. This is because the state of having been accomplished for a long time does not exceed these four. Although the distant and the near differ, the principle of the "four-in-one" is equal.
Regarding the phrase "By contemplating the mind, it can be understood," and so forth: this is because all [phenomena] manifest the ease of contemplating the single principle.

Nevertheless, one must have a brief understanding to demonstrate it as follows. The single mind and the three truths are one in principle; the single mind and the three contemplations are one in practice; the person who performs this contemplation is one; and the teaching that explains the object of this contemplation is one.
Furthermore, one should constantly contemplate that the three virtues—both subject and object—are each fourfold: the Dharmakāya is the principle, Prajñā is the teaching, and Vimukti is the practice.
The harmonious integration of these three dharmas constitutes the conventionally named person; this is the Tathāgata of contemplative practice.

Approximately six positions, each position being fourfold and one; in every thought-moment, each thought-moment is fourfold and one. Not a single form or a single fragrance is not fourfold and one. Contemplative practice such as this is the true samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
The mutual arising of mind and phenomena is the fourfold oneness from the perspective of cause and condition;
its difference from the three teachings is the fourfold oneness from the perspective of doctrine and contemplation;
its attainment since remote antiquity is the fourfold oneness from the perspective of the original ground.
Previously, I refuted the Guangzhai school precisely to establish the "Four and One.
This concludes the general explanation of the five chapters.
Next, from the section on "The Assembly Gathers" onwards, follows the formal, detailed exposition.
In the initial explanation of the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), the treatise first cites four accomplishments:
first, surrounding; second, preceding and following; third, making offerings; and fourth, honoring and praising.
The sūtra text omits the words "before and behind"; it should read "surrounded before and behind.
Master She remarked:
"Although this follows the treatise, it does not accord with the meaning of the sūtra. This was because Master She still harbored doubts regarding the translator.
However, our school generally relies upon the *Śāstra*, using it except for one or two instances where it is not applied in its entirety.

For example, regarding the three [categories] that do not require this refutation, the *Śāstra* explains the five phrases concerning "mere reflection" (*vitarka*) by means of eight phrases; it explains the five phrases praising the virtues of the Arhat by means of fifteen phrases; and it explains "difficult to understand" and "difficult to enter" by adding "difficult to awaken to," and so forth.
Therefore, adding [this qualification] results in no fault.
I have previously examined the three or two fascicles of that commentary; many of its points that were cause for apprehension have been resolved herein.

Among the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), this excludes the other three; since the desire to hear [the Dharma] differs from staying at an improper time, it is said to be "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*). How much more so, then, must one wait for this very sutra before it can be called "in accordance with the Dharma"?
If one discusses this generally, those who surround [the Buddha] according to their respective schools and capacities are all acting in accordance with the Dharma.
In the formal exposition, the author first refutes ancient views by directly stating that there are four groups beginning with the bhikṣus.

Some claim there are four groups beginning with devas and nāgas, and four groups beginning with Brahmā and Māra; yet, although such listings exist in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as among new and old traditions, they do not distinguish between ordinary beings and sages, the rebellious and the compliant, the provisional and the real, speech and silence, the subtle and the manifest, the shared and the distinct, or the combined and the solitary. Furthermore, regarding the bestowal and opening of the fundamental and the trace, these accounts lack any definitive purpose or conclusion.
The four categories now listed encompass all four types and include the ten pairs; thus, from ordinary beings and sages to the fundamental and the manifested, there is no confusion.
Furthermore, Master Shesheng said:
"Tiantai established the 'influential' and other assemblies; while there is doctrinal justification for them, there is no scriptural text, so they cannot yet be relied upon as authoritative."

If that is so, there is the position that where there is meaning but no text, one should not rely on it because of a lack of faith; should it then follow that where there is text but no meaning, one may rely upon it?

Now, we say: where there is both text and meaning, ordinary people employ it; where there is meaning but no text, the wise employ it; where there is text but no meaning, the ignorant employ it; and where there is neither text nor meaning, the deluded employ it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "Rely on the meaning, not on the words," which is precisely this point.

Thus, when compared to the inner, great, and ultimate reality, both the external and the provisional traces of the Lesser Vehicle possess names but lack true meaning; hence, the Buddha rebuked Kāśyapa, saying: "In the past, you heard only the name of Nirvāṇa, but you have not heard its meaning."

The Dharma Master has himself established two classes of noble beings—the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas—and two classes of ordinary beings—the various dragons, spirits, and human rulers. Now, he asks: do these four possess the four [qualities] of Tiantai or not?
If it were non-existent, what would it have to do with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
There would not even be anyone present who could benefit from the teaching, let alone those who initiate it and so forth.
Such a claim is untenable; if it does exist, it possesses both text and meaning—how can you say there is no text?
Therefore, when this sutra lists the assembly, it must necessarily include these four; this refers to the text.
In terms of meaning, there must necessarily be the four elements such as the "initiation" (nidāna); this refers to the meaning.
Possessing both text and meaning, it is entirely worthy of reliance and adherence.

The Dharma Master’s position—that there is no meaning but only the text—is itself subject to this very reproach; how much more so when the four meanings still pervade all the sutras. At present, one must speak of the "arousing" [of the potential], the "original and trace," the "provisional teaching," and the "causes and conditions. As for the sequence of these four: although the capacity [of the listener] may be aroused, it necessarily relies on a preliminary guide. Once the guide has aroused that capacity, the influence and response unfold extensively; yet, if the three benefits are entirely absent, there is no assembly for planting the seeds of affinity (*karmic connection*).
If you say there is no textual evidence, how could Mañjuśrī and Maitreya not be the initiators?
How could those who received predictions during the three assemblies not be the primary audience?
And apart from the initiators, how could the other great bodhisattvas not be the responsive echoes?
Setting aside those in the immediate assembly who have risen and departed, are they not nonetheless forming karmic connections?
Furthermore, within the miscellaneous assembly, although there may be no striking or stirring, one can still provide guidance; thus, they are collectively termed "initiators.
Although they do not constitute a permanent adornment, they can still provide assistance; thus, they are collectively termed "influences" and "echoes."
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states:
"And yet he is born into the five realms," which manifests his own nature as well as the meaning of the fourfold assembly he leads.
In the initial explanation of the introduction, there are the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Regarding the "first dharma," the internal virtues are first clarified.
The section beginning with "striking and uplifting" refers to external application.

It is called "expedient" (*upāya*) because it is established in response to sentient beings; it is called "strategy" (*māyā*) because it is formulated in accordance with what is appropriate. Because there is strategy within expedience, it is termed "expedient strategy."
True wisdom is internally integrated and responds appropriately without deliberation; thus it is called "wisdom-inspection" (*zhìjiàn*).
Because it inspects past roots of goodness that can be brought forth and perfected, it is named "knowing the occasion" (*zhījī*).
Because it adapts to circumstances without error, it is named "knowing the time" (*zhīshí*).

The meaning of the term "initiation" (*samutthāna*) should be understood as that which causes [something] to arise; it is used here to explain the name because it triggers the mechanism to bring [the action] forth, hence it is called "initiation.

In the initial passage, the first part explains "arising" (*sam*), while the section beginning with "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) explains "causing to arise" (*utthāna*). Alternatively, the first four characters provide the direct definition, while the subsequent four characters describe its functional capacity.
"Movement" (*dong*) also means "arising.
Furthermore, because it is split open and made to unfold, it is called "emerging" (*fa*); because it is stirred and set in motion by striking and uplifting it, it is called "arising" (*qi*).
This meaning encompasses both the agent and the object, as well as the self and the other.

Furthermore, it strikes the great compassion of equality, awakening the single goodness within the assembly; it raises up the great wisdom of non-duality, moving the three karmas of those who receive its benefit.

Moreover, it strikes the latent causes from past lives within this great assembly, awakening the wondrous benefits appropriate for their capacities; it proclaims the Great Teaching of the Tathāgata, shaking the deep-seated attachments of the congregation.

Furthermore, it is called "striking" (gī) because it strikes upon the Buddha’s great compassion; it is called "raising" (yāṅ) because it raises inquiries regarding the sacred intent; it is called "setting in motion" (fàndòng) because it causes one to hear what has not been heard before; it is called "accomplishing" (chéngbàn) because it enables those who hear it to achieve their fruition; and it is called "benefiting" (lìyì) because such fruition necessarily leads to awakening.

Next, regarding the illustration: the Great Powerful Elephant King topples the tree of the *dharmakāya* and reaches the ground of manifesting the *nirmāṇakāya*. He proclaims the reality of the One Vehicle and provides the karmic conditions for those whose capacities are nourished by wondrous practice. Following the passage beginning with "That is to say," the commentary on the integration states that the initiation of the five sequences benefits all sentient beings. Thus, we know that the assembly is never in vain; it is the mandate of the Great Powerful One. It is because of this assembly that the auspicious signs appear, culminating in the dialogue.

The term "etc. (等) includes the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*). Since the intent of the introduction has already been clarified and the formal exposition is about to begin, the original aspiration of the main doctrine is initiated within the introduction; thus, one can verify that this introduction does not extend throughout the entire root text. Although it is placed at the beginning of the sūtra, it is distinct from the root text itself. Nevertheless, while the initiation of both [the introduction and the root text] occurs in the *Īśvara*, the manifested event is not remote enough to be attributed to Mañjuśrī; because the long-standing origin is difficult to determine, it is entrusted solely to the Buddha.
Regarding the explanation of "being appropriate to the occasion" (*dangji*), there is also the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy, and the application.
First, concerning the principle: it is because there is an initiation that one can become appropriate to the occasion.
"Appropriate" (*dang*) means "to be fit for" or "to correspond to."
The character below is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng). "Sù" (宿) means to go.
"Zhí" (植) means to plant.

"Virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to the multitude of good deeds. Because it is the root of all good deeds, it is called the "Root of Virtue. Since goodness has a root, one is able to become a responsive capacity (*tāyin*). Through the functioning of great skillful means, the Buddha benefits sages and aids ordinary beings; thus, the Tathāgata’s threefold penetration describes them as having planted seeds in the past. Therefore, upon his initial attainment of the Way, he protected them from the suffering of extinction. Subsequently, in the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā periods, he considered the arising of their capacities. Thus, in this sutra, he first provides a brief teaching and then a detailed one. Through the three cycles of instruction, he encompasses all without exception, leading even those in the Root Chapter to the stage of the Stainless. Not differing by so much as a hair’s breadth from their past causes, they are able to give rise to realization within themselves; hence, they are called "responsive capacities" (*tāyin*).

Now, according to the assembly of Śākyas, the two characters "responsive" (dangji) both belong to those being transformed; yet, since it must be discussed in terms of the union of faculty and response, the principle logically encompasses both the agent and the object. For now, we shall follow the perspective of that which responds to those being transformed.

In the phrase "planted in former lives" (*sukṣipta-pūrva*), the character *jī* (mechanism/capacity) is first explained; in the phrase "convergence of conditions" (*pratyaya-sāmagrī*), the character *dāng* (destined/fitting) is next explained.
Furthermore, in the subsequent analogy, "like an abscess" (*piḍaka*) is used as a metaphor for the presence of a mechanism.
"Desire to burst forth" is a metaphor for that which can be brought into manifestation.

Because the Buddha, the Great Sage, and the assembly of initiators act in concert without prior consultation, afflictions and delusions are shattered, the conditions of the faculties ripen, the divisions of wisdom and virtue are formed, and the divisions of the Dharma-body are revealed.
"Non-arising" refers to the convergence below.
It does not mean that the capacity [of the response] moves toward the stimulus; rather, it means that the manifestation of the response coincides with the stimulus.

Since the manifestation of the response constitutes the manifest stimulus, one does not arise from the seat of "one emerging from the immeasurable," yet immediately hears the teaching of "the immeasurable returning to the one. Because all thereby ascend to the First Abode, it is called "attaining the Way."
This refers to the specific suitability [of the audience] according to their essential nature.
Generally speaking, however, it encompasses all six sense faculties and the five grades of practitioners.

Next, regarding the explanation of the "echoing and shadow-like" assembly: the physical form and voice of the transforming master must rely on companions as echoes and shadows; only then can the process of initiating and stimulating [the response] be accomplished. This is like an echo responding to a sound or a shadow following a form—this constitutes the application of the dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis.

Regarding the first section on the Dharma: the first two phrases clarify the basis of the influence and response, while the subsequent passage beginning with "concealing his... clarifies the traces of the one who provides assistance. Since that which is assisted is unique, he is called the "Dharma King."
Those who are able to assist demonstrate the cause, the gradual process, the beginning, and the end; these are the majestic demeanors of the various sages.

Because they demonstrate the cause, ancient Buddhas conceal their ultimate state to manifest the practice of cultivation; because they demonstrate the gradual process, the Dharmakāya remains secretly perfect while manifesting the partial and the small. All of these serve to support and assist the Dharma King Śākyamuni.
"Kuang" (匡) means to rectify.
The *Shifa* (Method of Posthumous Titles) states:
"A sincere heart and great magnanimity are called Kuang."
"Assistant" (*fu*) means to provide support.

With a loyal heart, one assists the sovereign in discerning that the capacities of things have their proper place, thereby yielding the merit of righteous transformation; hence it is called "echo and shadow."

As for the subsequent analogy: it is like a star that illuminates alone in the darkness; its function is merely to assist the moon, manifesting its virtue through silent support. Therefore, it is said that although it performs no deliberate action, it brings about immense benefit.
The *Mahā-śāstra* asks:
For what reason do the bhikṣus always follow the World-Honored One?
It answers:

Just as a patient’s recovery following a physician’s treatment manifests the physician’s merit, here we see that even those who practice according to the reality [of the teachings] still possess the formal manifestations of influence;

how much more so for the Buddhas of the Dharma-body, who manifest forms to assist in transformation? Thus we know that the fourfold assembly is like those with light illnesses being cured, while the eight classes of beings are like those with grave illnesses being cured; both light and heavy cases possess the provisional and real manifestations of influence.

Next, to explain "establishing a karmic connection" (*kyōen*): "Connection" (*ketsu*) refers to the initial structuring of the capacity for awakening; "condition" (*en*) refers to the supportive conditions that enable its completion. Thus, it constitutes the first sprout of the three virtues to be cultivated and attained in the future.
Because it lacks the first three types of benefit, it is called "establishing a karmic connection" (*kyōen*); that is, it is the remainder following the aforementioned three assemblies.
Thus, this single connection possesses two meanings: namely, assisting the present and assisting the future.

Within this, first, the absence [of these qualities] is distinguished in contrast to the preceding three: "lack of power" distinguishes it from the initiating cause; "virtue is not" distinguishes it from the contributing influence; and "yet there is transgression" clarifies that it is not suitable for those who are ready for the teaching.
All that initiates the assembly possesses two meanings:
first, leading [beings] to the place of assembly; second, striking the Buddha to perfect their spiritual capacity (*ki*).
Since the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas possess these two functions, it is said they "are able" to do so.
However, those who form a karmic connection with them lack its benefits; hence it is said, "lacking power.
"Stability" (鎮) refers to being grave and weighty, which is internal virtue.
"Adornment" (嚴) refers to being majestic and ornate, which is external deportment.

Since internal virtue is already lofty, external deportment must necessarily be orderly; as the solemn adornment of transformative activities brings glory to the Master's function, those who form karmic connections find nothing [of their own] therein; thus it is said, "powerless," and so forth.
Furthermore, one must stabilize them with gravity and subdue them with severity; once they are stabilized and subdued, the path of transformation can be implemented—hence the phrase "the use of.
Those who have merely established these conditions benefit themselves only slightly; how then could they stabilize or subdue others?
Therefore, it is said that "virtue is absent. Regarding the terms "concealed" (*fù*) and "leaking" (*lòu*), the character *fù* is pronounced in the entering tone.

Because one lacks the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), it is like a vessel turned upside down; because one lacks the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is like a vessel that has already leaked; because one lacks the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), it is like a vessel that is soiled and impure. Just as a vessel, though upright and complete, is discarded by its user because it is soiled and impure, the text concludes by stating: "the three wisdoms do not arise."

Regarding the phrase "in this present life" and so forth: although one may currently hear [the teaching], it is not yet called wisdom (*prajñā*). If even the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is absent, how could there be the wisdoms of reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*)?

This refers generally to the six sense faculties and the five grades [of beings]; specifically, it refers to those such as the five thousand who rose up and departed. Thus, although those who rose up and departed lacked the three types of wisdom, they received the seeds within their nature and were able to become "those who have fastened the jewel. Therefore, one knows that there was no benefit for the world during the stage of contemplative practice; hence it is said, "there was no benefit through the four *siddhāntas*."

According to these stages, all four *siddhāntas* may be called "appropriate to the capacity" (*yathābhavyatā*). Thus, from the five levels [of faith] onward, there is the benefit for the world (*loka-saṃvṛti*);
from the six sense organs onward, there is the benefit of human instruction and remediation (*puruṣa-vyākaraṇa-pratipakṣa*);
and from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward, there is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, at the end of the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (Sui-xi-pin) below, even a single phrase or a single verse serves as a karmic connection for those present who are suited to the teaching.

However, hearing a brief exposition may yield a benefit exceeding that of a single phrase or verse; thus, regardless of the quantity heard, as long as one has not yet entered the [Five] Stages (Wu-pin), it is all termed a "karmic connection. Consequently, prior to these five stages, there is no longer the presence of the three types of wisdom (san-hui) or the fourfold benefits (si-xi).

Because there is no hearing, there is no world; because there is no thought, there is no person; because there is no cultivation, there is no antidote; because there is no realization, there is no ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Thus, the ultimate truth has both a general and a specific sense: it is general across the five stages and specific to the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*). Therefore, the expression "attaining deliverance" also has both a general and a specific sense, which is precisely the general and specific aspects of the ultimate truth.
Thus, although the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold meanings) apply universally, they ultimately result in distinct stages for establishing karmic connections (*karmabandha*).
The phrase "merely acts as" below correctly demonstrates the various characteristics of those who establish such connections.

Regarding the enumeration of sixteen groups starting with "bhikṣus," if one relies on the text, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are present only within the assembly of bhikṣus; and although there is no explicit text regarding the nuns requesting the Dharma, the subsequent passage contains signs of them requesting a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). As for the two lay assemblies, although there is no direct textual evidence, by analogy they should be included, for once they have reached the site of the assembly, they must necessarily be guided by those who manifest through skillful means (*upāya*).
If this is the case for the two assemblies, it is likewise for the eight classes of beings.

Now, because we speak only of the "four assemblies" from the perspective of general characteristics, one should know that to say they are subsumed solely within the four groups beginning with the bhikṣus is incomplete; to claim there is no scriptural authority for this is a profound failure of understanding.

Next, regarding "this is" and subsequently "concerning the three teachings," this includes a discussion of the former teachings; the transmission and citations of the five flavors can be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Regarding "the fundamental and the trace are understandable": if we consider them in terms of essence and function, the fundamental resides in the most honored and ultimate state, or as the Dharma-body of the profound stages; the trace consists of the four teachings and their sixteen assemblies.

Regarding the statement that "observing the mind clarifies the stages and takes the five grades as those who have formed a karmic connection," this is spoken in terms of the practice of contemplation; therefore, it uses the stage of names and the stage of contemplative practice as the point of forming a karmic connection, because among those who are suited to the teaching, one enters the stage of the first abode immediately within the stage of influence.

One should know that the first stage possesses two meanings: those who have entered previously are merely termed "echoes and reflections," and this same principle applies even to those who, upon hearing the sutra, transcend directly into subsequent stages.

If those who have newly entered [the path] attain this, they serve as those who are suited to the occasion, as well as those who act as influences and those who provide inspiration—just like those followers who vowed to propagate the sutra.

As for the phrase "and so forth," it refers to distinguishing these four types to establish the differences in the levels of their contemplative practice; it is because upon reaching this stage, all are capable of becoming these four kinds of assemblies.

Even those five thousand who rose and departed were still able to form a karmic connection; thus we know that it is not merely a matter of names or the five grades of practice. Therefore, based on contemplative practice (*guanxing*), one can explain "surrounding" with ease.

The initial passage possesses all four *siddhāntas*, though they are not explicitly manifest; one should infer them from what precedes. "Descending beneath the Pure Abodes" corresponds to the Worldly (*loka*) perspective;

"transforming into human form" corresponds to the Personal (*puruṣa*) perspective; "being taken as a model by people" corresponds to the Therapeutic (*pratikāra*) perspective; and "having paid obeisance, they listen to the Dharma" corresponds to the Ultimate (*paramārtha*) perspective.
The section "Manifesting the Four Gates" sets aside the provisional teachings.

If one were to discuss the assembly directly according to the specific teaching at hand, there would naturally be Buddhas within each of those various teachings; however, here we follow the perspective of the ultimate meaning of the surrounding [assembly], which manifests the movement of the faculties through the four gates of the three teachings, and because they move, they perceive the principle.
At the time of the *Immeasurable Meanings*, it was still partial and small; this served as a pre-indication that one would later hear the four gates of the Perfect Teaching.
When comparing the present with the past, the meanings of the four teachings are complete; therefore, it simply says "by analogy."

Therefore, we know that the teachings of the past were not without the four gates; it was simply that the capacities of those to be taught had not yet been activated. However, when those who were previously dull and unrefined reach this point, they are then said to have their "Great Capacity" activated.

If one who was originally of the Perfect [Vehicle] reaches this stage and further progresses, this is also called "activation," though it is not distinct [from the others]; yet, by virtue of its distinction, it receives the name of the "four gates."
